history.hpi: 62-year-old male was playing in a recreational softball game when teammates report he suddenly grabbed his chest, said he felt "lightheaded," and collapsed to the ground while standing near first base. A teammate who is an off-duty ICU nurse recognized the collapse as cardiac arrest, called 911, and began chest compressions immediately — no more than 15-20 seconds after the patient went down. No AED was available on site. Bystander CPR has been ongoing since collapse.
pastMedical: Prior myocardial infarction 3 years ago with drug-eluting stent placement (LAD)
history.lastOralIntake: Light breakfast (toast, coffee) approximately 4 hours prior to collapse
history.events: Witnessed sudden collapse during a recreational softball game; teammate began bystander CPR within seconds; 911 called immediately; no AED on scene.

scene.dispatch: Respond to the community softball complex for a 62-year-old male, collapsed, unconscious and unresponsive, bystander CPR in progress.
scene.location: Public softball field, infield near first base, community recreation complex
scene.time: Saturday afternoon, mid-summer, warm and sunny
scene.safety: Open public park with a gathering crowd of players and spectators; ensure clear access lane for equipment and stretcher; no AED on site
scene.bystanders: Teammate (off-duty ICU nurse) performing chest compressions; several teammates and spectators gathered, one directing traffic for the ambulance
visualCues: Patient supine on infield dirt, softball uniform, cleats still on
Bystander performing chest compressions, visibly fatigued
Small crowd of teammates gathered around, one waving in the ambulance
No AED visible anywhere on scene
Bat and glove dropped near the patient

phases.name: Initial Contact
phases.description: Crew arrives to find a 62-year-old male supine on the infield, unresponsive, with a bystander performing chest compressions. Rapid assessment confirms no pulse, no respirations, and agonal/absent breathing.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but unprotected; no spontaneous respirations
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic; occasional agonal gasps noted by bystander prior to EMS arrival
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No palpable carotid or radial pulse; bystander compressions ongoing
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: None – flaccid, unresponsive to painful stimuli
otherFindings: Bystander CPR in progress, adequate depth/rate per nurse bystander report
No AED applied prior to EMS arrival

expectedActions.shortAction: Confirm pulselessness and apnea rapidly; do not delay treatment for full assessment
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Assessment: The patient in cardiac arrest requires a prompt balance of treatment and assessment. In cases of cardiac arrest, assessments should be focused and limited to obtaining enough information to reveal the patient is pulseless. Once pulselessness is discovered, treatment should be initiated immediately, and any further history must be obtained by bystanders while treatment is ongoing.
expectedActions.rationale: Prevents delay of compressions/defibrillation while gathering unnecessary history.

transitions.condition: Crew takes over chest compressions from the bystander without delay while a second rescuer applies defibrillator pads and begins rhythm analysis.
Crew pauses compressions to perform a full head-to-toe assessment or gather extended history before taking over CPR, interrupting effective compressions.

phases.name: CPR & Pads Applied
phases.description: Crew has taken over high-quality chest compressions from the bystander and applied defibrillator pads. Monitor confirms coarse ventricular fibrillation.
phases.triggerCondition: EMS crew immediately takes over compressions from the fatigued bystander while a second rescuer applies pads; the monitor is analyzed without interrupting compressions and confirms coarse VF.

clinicalPresentation.airway: OPA inserted; NRB/BVM being set up
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic; passive ventilation via NRB during initial compression cycles
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No palpable pulse; effective compressions in progress, rate ~110/min, full recoil
otherFindings: Defibrillator pads applied in anterolateral position
Coarse VF confirmed on rhythm analysis

expectedActions.shortAction: Take over compressions from bystander; apply pads and analyze rhythm without delay
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Initiate chest compressions in cases with no bystander chest compressions or take over compressions from bystanders while a second rescuer is setting up the AED or defibrillator. If adequate, uninterrupted bystander CPR has been performed or if the patient arrests in front of the EMS clinicians, immediately proceed with rhythm analysis and defibrillation, if appropriate.
expectedActions.rationale: Minimizing hands-off time preserves coronary perfusion pressure.

expectedActions.shortAction: Maintain compression rate 100-120/min, depth 2-2.4 inches, allow full chest recoil
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: A rate of greater than 100 and less than 120 compressions/minute. Depth of at least 2 inches (5 cm) and less than 2.4 inches (6 cm) for adults and children. Allow for complete chest recoil (avoid leaning). Minimize interruptions in compressions.
expectedActions.rationale: High-quality CPR is the primary driver of survival in shockable rhythms.

expectedActions.shortAction: Apply passive oxygenation via NRB with OPA for first compression cycles; do not interrupt compressions
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Passive ventilation: High flow oxygen is applied via a non-rebreather mask with an oropharyngeal airway. This may be applied for the first 3–4 compression cycles (6–8 minutes), after which one may consider BVM ventilation or placement of an advanced airway.
expectedActions.rationale: Adult airway management is secondary to compressions/defibrillation and should not interrupt either.

transitions.condition: VF confirmed on rhythm analysis; defibrillator charged without interrupting compressions and first shock delivered per protocol energy setting.

phases.name: First Shock Delivered
phases.description: Crew delivers the first defibrillation and immediately resumes chest compressions for a full 2-minute cycle without pausing for a pulse check.
phases.triggerCondition: Defibrillator pre-charged during ongoing compressions; compressions paused only momentarily for shock delivery, then resumed immediately for a 2-minute cycle while IV/IO access is obtained.

clinicalPresentation.airway: OPA in place; BVM ventilation being considered
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No palpable pulse; compressions resumed immediately post-shock
otherFindings: IV access being attempted in the AC without interrupting compressions
Single shock delivered; compressions resumed within seconds

expectedActions.shortAction: Defibrillate at 120 J (first shock, Zoll biphasic per protocol)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Defibrillation dosing should follow manufacturer's recommendation in the case of biphasic defibrillators. If the manufacturer's recommendation is unknown, use highest setting possible. Zoll – Adult – 120 J, 150 J, 200 J.
expectedActions.rationale: Prompt defibrillation for a shockable rhythm is a primary determinant of survival.

expectedActions.shortAction: Resume compressions immediately post-shock; no pulse check for 2 minutes
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Chest compressions should resume immediately after defibrillation attempts with no pauses for pulse checks for 2 minutes regardless of the rhythm displayed on the cardiac monitor.
expectedActions.rationale: Avoids unnecessary peri-shock pauses that reduce coronary perfusion pressure.

expectedActions.shortAction: Obtain IV/IO access without interrupting chest compressions
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: IV or IO access without interrupting chest compressions.
expectedActions.rationale: Vascular access is needed for medication administration if arrest continues, but must not disrupt compressions.

expectedActions.shortAction: Pre-charge defibrillator during compressions to minimize peri-shock pause
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: All attempts should be made to prevent avoidable interruptions in chest compressions, such as pre-charging the defibrillator and hovering over the chest, rather than stepping away during defibrillations.
expectedActions.rationale: Reduces hands-off time between the end of a compression cycle and shock delivery.

transitions.condition: At the 2-minute rhythm/pulse check following the single shock, an organized rhythm with a palpable central pulse is identified.
At the 2-minute rhythm/pulse check, the monitor still shows VF with no palpable pulse, indicating refractory VF requiring escalation.

phases.name: ROSC Achieved
phases.description: After one 2-minute cycle of CPR following the single shock, the pulse/rhythm check reveals an organized sinus tachycardia with a palpable carotid pulse. Compressions are stopped and post-ROSC care begins.
phases.triggerCondition: The scheduled 2-minute rhythm/pulse check after the single shock reveals return of spontaneous circulation: organized rhythm on the monitor with a palpable carotid pulse and rising SpO2.

clinicalPresentation.airway: OPA in place; BVM ventilations ongoing
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic to shallow agonal respirations; being ventilated via BVM
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Palpable carotid and weak radial pulse; skin color improving
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Minimal spontaneous movement; withdraws to pain
otherFindings: Crew immediately transitions to post-ROSC care

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize ROSC; stop compressions once organized rhythm with pulse confirmed
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: If at any time during this period of resuscitation the patient regains return of spontaneous circulation, treat per Adult Post-ROSC Care Guideline.
expectedActions.rationale: Continuing compressions after ROSC is unnecessary and can be harmful.

expectedActions.shortAction: Support airway/breathing and circulation; identify likely cause of arrest
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Perform general patient assessment attempting to identify cause of cardiac arrest. Support life-threatening problems associated with airway, breathing, and circulation.
expectedActions.rationale: Post-ROSC patients remain unstable and require ongoing ABC support.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

expectedActions.shortAction: Monitor closely for re-arrest via cardiac monitor, EtCO2, and perfusion signs
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Monitor closely for recurrence of cardiac arrest using clinical and adjunctive criteria such as cardiac monitoring, EtCO2 monitoring, and physical signs of perfusion.
expectedActions.rationale: A significant percentage of post-ROSC patients re-arrest and require rapid recognition.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

transitions.condition: Crew transitions into structured post-ROSC management: oxygenation/ventilation titration, 12-lead acquisition, glucose check, and transport planning.

phases.name: Post-ROSC Care & Transport
phases.description: Patient remains unresponsive but hemodynamically improving. Crew titrates oxygenation and ventilation, acquires a 12-lead EKG to screen for STEMI, checks glucose, and prepares for transport to an appropriate receiving facility.
phases.triggerCondition: Following confirmed ROSC, the crew moves into structured post-arrest care per the Adult Post-ROSC Care Guideline while preparing the patient for transport.

clinicalPresentation.airway: OPA/BVM in place, well tolerated; SGA placement considered per local protocol
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Assisted ventilations at 8-10/min via BVM, chest rise adequate
clinicalPresentation.circulation: Palpable radial pulse, improving perfusion, no signs of re-arrest
clinicalPresentation.motorFunction: Abnormal flexion (decorticate posturing) to painful stimuli
otherFindings: 12-lead EKG acquired, no obvious ST elevation identified

expectedActions.shortAction: Titrate oxygen to SpO2 94-98%; avoid hyperoxygenation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer oxygen as appropriate with a target of achieving 94–98% saturation. Do not hyperoxygenate.
expectedActions.rationale: Hyperoxia post-ROSC is associated with worse neurologic outcomes.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

expectedActions.shortAction: Ventilate 8-10 breaths/min; target EtCO2 35-45 mmHg, avoid hyperventilation
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Do not hyperventilate. Maintain a ventilation rate of 8–10 breaths per minute, targeting an EtCO2 of 35–45 mmHg.
expectedActions.rationale: Hyperventilation reduces cerebral perfusion and can precipitate re-arrest.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

expectedActions.shortAction: Acquire 12-lead EKG within 10 minutes to screen for STEMI; transmit and notify receiving hospital if positive
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: It is imperative that EMS clinicians routinely acquire a 12-lead EKG within 10 minutes for all patients exhibiting signs and symptoms of ACS. Advance notification should be provided to the receiving hospital for patients identified as having a STEMI.
expectedActions.rationale: A cardiac cause is the most likely etiology of this witnessed VF arrest and must be actively screened for.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Chest Pain/Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS)/ST-segment Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI)

expectedActions.shortAction: Transport to a cath-capable facility if STEMI or reversible cardiac cause identified
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Post-cardiac arrest patients with evidence or interpretation consistent with ST elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI/acute MI) should be transported preferably to a facility capable of emergent cardiac catheterization or, as a secondary option, to a STEMI receiving facility based upon local resources and system of care.
expectedActions.rationale: Ensures the patient reaches definitive cardiac care as quickly as possible.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

expectedActions.shortAction: Check blood glucose; treat per Hypoglycemia Guideline if low, notify hospital if high
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Check blood glucose. If hypoglycemic, treat per Hypoglycemia Guideline. If hyperglycemic, notify hospital on arrival.
expectedActions.rationale: Glucose derangement can be a contributing or complicating factor post-arrest.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

expectedActions.shortAction: Avoid hyperthermia; do not apply warm blankets or excessive heat exposure
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Avoid hyperthermia (temperature greater than 37.5° C or 99.5° F) by avoiding excessive environmental heat exposure, warm blankets, etc.
expectedActions.rationale: Fever worsens neurologic outcomes after cardiac arrest.
expectedActions.protocolReference: MATC: Adult Post-ROSC (Return of Spontaneous Circulation) Care

phases.name: Compressions Delayed
phases.description: Crew pauses to perform a full assessment before taking over compressions, allowing a prolonged hands-off interval. Perfusion continues to deteriorate as fibrillation coarseness begins to diminish.
phases.triggerCondition: Rather than immediately taking over CPR from the fatigued bystander, the crew spends time performing a full head-to-toe exam and gathering extended history before starting compressions, producing a significant hands-off interval.

clinicalPresentation.airway: Patent but unprotected, no interventions yet
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic, no ventilatory support being provided
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No compressions in progress; no pulse; perfusion continuing to deteriorate
otherFindings: Bystander has stopped compressions, exhausted, awaiting crew

expectedActions.shortAction: Recognize delay; immediately resume compressions and apply pads without further assessment
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: In cases of cardiac arrest, assessments should be focused and limited to obtaining enough information to reveal the patient is pulseless. Once pulselessness is discovered, treatment should be initiated immediately, and any further history must be obtained by bystanders while treatment is ongoing.
expectedActions.rationale: Every second without compressions in VF reduces the likelihood of successful defibrillation and survival.

phases.name: Refractory VF
phases.description: The 2-minute rhythm/pulse check following the first shock shows persistent coarse VF with no pulse, requiring escalation to a second shock, epinephrine, and consideration of antiarrhythmic therapy.
phases.triggerCondition: Despite one defibrillation and 2 minutes of high-quality CPR, the rhythm check reveals persistent VF without ROSC, indicating shock-refractory VF requiring escalation per protocol.

clinicalPresentation.airway: OPA in place, BVM ventilation ongoing
clinicalPresentation.breathing: Apneic; BVM ventilations continuing without interruption to compressions
clinicalPresentation.circulation: No palpable pulse; compressions ongoing, IV/IO access established
otherFindings: Rhythm check at 2 minutes shows persistent coarse VF
IV/IO access now established for medication administration

expectedActions.shortAction: Deliver second defibrillation at 150 J (Zoll biphasic escalation)
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Zoll – Adult – 120 J, 150 J, 200 J.
expectedActions.rationale: Escalating energy is used for subsequent shocks in refractory VF per the Zoll biphasic sequence.

expectedActions.shortAction: Epinephrine 1 mg IV/IO (fixed adult dose, 0.1 mg/kg capped at max 1 mg); repeat q3-5min
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Administer epinephrine (0.1 mg/kg, maximum dose 1 mg) IV/IO during the first or second round of compressions.
expectedActions.rationale: Early epinephrine improves the likelihood of ROSC in refractory arrest.

expectedActions.shortAction: Consider Amiodarone 300 mg IV/IO for shock-refractory VF/pulseless VT
expectedActions.protocolExcerpt: Amiodarone 300mg, followed by 150mg 4-6 min later if still in refractory VF and pulseless VT.
expectedActions.rationale: Antiarrhythmic therapy may facilitate restoration of a perfusing rhythm in shock-refractory VF.
